title: Three agents, one blackboard, 21,800 tokens
intro: The same UCC risk report split across a lien-researcher, a related-party-researcher and a report-writer. Each pattern moves the same findings between windows — and the thing that decides whether the writer's window survives is not which pattern you picked, but what you allowed to travel.

provenance.source: a narrated 3-agent UCC pipeline; window sizes and token counts are plausible inventions, not measurements. The successor-course figures quoted in step 3 are real and are cited in prose, not as data

foot: This walks M26's Containing the Context Explosion — share summaries not raw context, scope each agent's reads, enforce the boundary between windows.

steps.title: One task, three windows
narrative: Take the risk report from M25 and give each branch of its DAG to a specialist. The lien-researcher runs 2a_liens, the related-party-researcher runs 2b_related, the report-writer runs 3_score and 4_format. The two researchers run in parallel, which is the whole reason to split.

But the split creates something the single agent did not have: three separate loop contexts (M24), and findings that now have to physically move between them. The orchestration is the easy half. The context flow is where these systems come apart.

The researchers are already heavy on their own. The lien-researcher pulls 12,900 tokens of FL, TX and GA filings; the related-party-researcher pulls 6,400 tokens of corporate registry records. That weight is fine — it is being read where it was retrieved. The question is how much of it is allowed to leave.
steps.youDo: For each agent in your system, write down what it retrieves and what it must hand on. If those two lists are the same list, you have not designed the sharing yet.

steps.title: The blackboard fills with raw filings
narrative: The first implementation is a blackboard: both researchers write what they found to a shared store and the writer reads it. Simple, and it works on the test fixture with two filings.

In production each researcher writes its retrieved context to the board — the filings themselves, not the conclusions drawn from them. So the board becomes 19,300 tokens and the writer's window becomes 21,800 against a 16,000-token budget. It overflows at 136%, the tail is truncated, and the report ships without the related-party section because that is what fell off the end.

The failure is not the pattern. A blackboard is a fine choice here. The failure is that the researchers shared their context when the writer needed their conclusions, and shared context grows with agents times steps while conclusions do not.

steps.title: The same task under three patterns
narrative: Run the identical work through all three. Hub-and-spoke: a coordinator delegates and collects, so the workers stay clean and the hub holds everything — 22,500 tokens if the workers return raw, 3,290 if they return findings. Blackboard: 21,800 at the writer with raw writes, 2,590 with shaped summaries and scoped reads. Message passing: 2,590, scoped by construction, with nobody holding the whole picture.

Read down the table and the pattern is not the variable. Hub-spoke with raw returns and blackboard with raw writes are within 700 tokens of each other; hub-spoke with shaped returns and message passing are within 700 of each other. What travels matters roughly ten times more than the topology it travels over.

The hub-with-raw-returns row is the one worth taking seriously, because it is measured. The successor course graded ten strategies on ten questions and found sub-agent isolation the most expensive of all of them — a median 1,805 input tokens against naive's 1,696, so delegating cost more than simply sending everything. The reason is exactly this row: the sub-agent's work comes back as a roughly 1,700-token tool-result layer in the parent's window. You paid for the sub-agent's context and then paid again to receive its output.
steps.claudeSays: Isolation moved the work out of my window. It did not move the work's output out of my window, and that is what I was billed for.
steps.youDo: Measure the size of what your sub-agent returns, not just what it was spared. Delegation that returns a transcript is a cost transfer, not a saving.

steps.title: Ninety tokens cross the boundary
narrative: The fix is one line per researcher. Keep the 19,300 tokens of filings and registry records where they were retrieved and where they are actually read, and write to the shared space only what the writer's task needs: debtor ACME: 7 active liens across 3 states; 1 related entity (ACME HOLDINGS FL LLC, 3 liens). That is 52 tokens from one researcher and 38 from the other.

The writer's window goes from 21,800 to 2,590 — 16% of its budget instead of 136% — and the related-party section is in the report, because nothing was truncated. The researchers' windows do not change at all. Total across all three windows falls from 46,100 to 26,890.

Add the boundary and you are done: an agent reads the board by scope, not wholesale, and the scope is checked the way a tenant is checked (M23), so one agent's state cannot arrive in another's window by default. The rule for the whole module is short — heavy data stays where it is used; only conclusions cross a boundary — and it holds for all three topologies, which is why it is the rule and the topology is a preference.
steps.claudeSays: I now receive ninety tokens and produce the same report, including the section that used to be truncated off the end.
steps.youDo: Put a size assertion on your shared store: assert len(tokenize(payload)) < 200 on every write. Anything that fails it is context masquerading as a finding.

views.text: Nothing was compressed and no researcher did less work. The only change is that a conclusion crossed the boundary instead of the evidence for it. Pick your topology on control and awareness — but whichever you pick, share summaries, scope every read, and keep one agent's context out of another's window by construction rather than by convention.
